summary: Defines managed objects for the IP Traffic Flow Security additions to IKEv2 and IPsec, in the older SNMP MIB format. It provides a read-only version of the objects from the YANG module in RFC 9348.

eli5.summary: It is a read-only dashboard, in an older style, for looking at how a privacy feature on a network device is doing.

questions: mib for ip traffic flow security
how to monitor ip-tfs with snmp
is the ip-tfs mib read only
subtitle: A read-only SNMP MIB for watching IP Traffic Flow Security on IPsec tunnels.

tldr.problem: IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) improves traffic confidentiality on IPsec tunnels, but operators whose tools speak SNMP had no standard way to see how it is configured or performing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IP-TRAFFIC-FLOW-SECURITY-MIB, a read-only MIB module derived from the YANG model in RFC 9348, with a configuration table and three statistics tables indexed per Security Association.
tldr.outcome: Existing network management systems can read IP-TFS operational data over SNMP. Nothing in the module can be written, so SNMP SET cannot change it.

today: RFC 9349 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its objects mirror the operational data of the YANG model in RFC 9348.

sections.title: Purpose and Place in the Management Framework
sections.content:
This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for network management protocols. IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS), defined in RFC 9347, is a set of enhancements to an IPsec tunnel Security Association (SA) that provide improved traffic confidentiality.

The objects here are the same as those in RFC 9348, except that only operational or state data is supported. Making that data available over SNMP lets existing network management systems monitor IP-TFS. The YANG data model is the reference point for the managed objects.

The RFC notes that an IETF MIB model for IPsec was never standardized. The structures defined here could be adapted to existing proprietary MIB implementations where SNMP is used to manage networks.

The module is written in SMIv2 (STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580), and the overall Internet-Standard Management Framework is described in RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Some network tools only understand an older way of asking devices questions. This document lets those tools check on a privacy feature too.

sections.title: Overview of the Model
sections.content:
The MIB gives access to operational parameters of IP-TFS. IP-TFS configures a Security Association for tunnel mode IPsec with characteristics that improve traffic confidentiality and reduce bandwidth efficiency loss.

The document builds on the concepts and management model of RFC 9348 and assumes familiarity with the IPsec concepts in RFC 4301 and IP-TFS in RFC 9347. It reuses the RFC 9348 management model and lets SNMP systems read operational objects, which include configured objects.

Everything is organized per SA: each table is indexed by an SA index, an Integer32 in the range 1 to 16777215. The RFC recommends assigning values contiguously, starting from 1.
sections.eli5: Every secret tunnel gets its own numbered page of notes, and the dashboard reads those pages.

sections.title: The MIB Tree and Its Tables
sections.content:
The module is registered as iptfsMIB at 1.3.6.1.2.1.500 in the tree diagram, with the object identifier value 246 under mib-2 given in the MIB text and recorded with IANA. Under it, iptfsMIBObjects holds four groups, each with one table.

  • iptfsConfigTable shows the IP-TFS configuration of an SA.
  • ipsecStatsTable holds basic IPsec counters: txPkts, txOctets, txDropPkts, rxPkts, rxOctets and rxDropPkts.
  • iptfsInnerStatsTable counts the user (inner) packets: sent and received packets and octets, plus rxIncompleteInnerPkts.
  • iptfsOuterStatsTable counts the outer IP-TFS packets, including padding and errors.

All accessible objects have MAX-ACCESS read-only, shown as r-n in the tree. A conformance section defines a compliance statement and four object groups, one per table.
sections.eli5: There are four notebooks per tunnel: one for settings, one for plain packet counts, one for the real messages inside, and one for the wrapping and padding outside.

sections.title: Configuration Objects
sections.content:
The configuration table reports how IP-TFS is set up on an SA. Some objects apply on transmission and some on reception.

  • congestionControl: when true, the default, enables the on-the-wire exchange of data required by congestion control as defined in RFC 5348. When false, IP-TFS sends fixed-size packets at a constant rate.
  • usePathMtuDiscovery and outerPacketSize: whether the packet size is discovered or configured, and the size of the outer encapsulating packet, the IP packet containing ESP.
  • l2FixedRate and l3FixedRate: the target bit rate in bits per second, specified as a layer 2 wire rate or a layer 3 packet rate. If congestion control is enabled, the rate may be adjusted down.
  • dontFragment: disables fragmentation across consecutive tunnel packets, so inner packets too large for an outer packet are dropped.
  • maxAggregationTime: the longest an inner packet can be held before transmission. Packets that would be held longer are dropped rather than queued.
  • windowSize: the maximum number of out-of-order packets a receiver will reorder. The value 0 disables reordering.
  • sendImmediately: send inner packets as soon as possible without waiting for lost or misordered outer packets. This reduces delay but can amplify out-of-order delivery.
  • lostPacketTimerInterval: how long a receiver waits for a missing packet before considering it lost. Setting it too low can impact reordering and reassembly.
sections.eli5: These are the knobs on the tunnel: how big the packets are, how fast to send, how long to wait for stragglers. This document only lets you read where the knobs are set.

sections.title: Statistics Objects
sections.content:
The statistics tables are all Counter64 values. The IPsec statistics count outbound and inbound packets, bytes and drops for an SA.

The inner statistics count whole user packets only: a fragmented packet counts as one packet, and octet counts exclude padding. rxIncompleteInnerPkts counts inner packets that were incomplete, usually because fragments were not received, and possibly because of misordering or errors in received outer packets.

The outer statistics separate padding into two kinds, in both transmit and receive directions: outer packets that carried data plus some padding (ExtraPad), and packets that were all padding with no inner packet data (AllPad). Two more counters cover outer packets dropped due to errors (rxErroredPkts) and outer packets missing, as indicated by a missing sequence number (rxMissedPkts).
sections.eli5: The counters tally how many real messages and how much filler went through, and how many arrived broken or went missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module has no objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through direct SNMP SET operations. For implications of write configuration, the RFC points to RFC 9347.

Some objects may still be sensitive. The RFC singles out iptfsInnerStatsTable and iptfsOuterStatsTable: access to the inner and outer statistics can reveal information that IP-TFS obscures, such as the true activity of the flows. It is therefore important to control even GET and NOTIFY access, and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire.

Implementations SHOULD provide the security features of the SNMPv3 framework. Those claiming compliance to SNMPv3 MUST fully support authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with the AES cipher, and MAY support the Transport Security Model with a secure transport such as SSH or TLS/DTLS. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: You cannot change anything with this dashboard, but peeking at the counters could reveal how busy a hidden tunnel is, so only trusted people should be allowed to look.
